title: Bài sưu tầm 114 - Passage 1: The Secrets of the Peat Bog Bodies
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 114

The Secrets of the Peat Bog Bodies

Paragraph 1. Across the waterlogged peat bogs of northwestern Europe—spanning Denmark, northern Germany, the British Isles, and the Low Countries—peat cutters and archaeologists have unearthed hundreds of remarkably preserved human remains dating from the European Iron Age (c. 500 BCE to 400 CE). Known colloquially as 'bog bodies', these ancient individuals display an eerie, lifelike preservation that defies the natural processes of decay. Unlike dry desert mummies or ice-bound freeze-dried corpses, bog bodies retain their soft dermal tissues, internal organs, delicate fingernails, intricate skin pores, and facial expressions, providing an unprecedented biological window into the lives and violent deaths of our prehistoric ancestors.

Paragraph 2. The miraculous preservation of these ancient remains is driven by the unique environmental chemistry of wetland peat bogs. Peat bogs are stagnant, wetland ecosystems dominated by Sphagnum moss. As successive layers of moss die and compress over millennia under waterlogged conditions, an environment entirely devoid of oxygen is created. In this anaerobic setting, normal aerobic microorganisms that consume human flesh cannot survive. Furthermore, Sphagnum moss releases a complex polysaccharide called sphagnan into the surrounding water. Sphagnan acts as an extraordinary natural tanning agent: it immobilizes metal ions, effectively depriving surviving bacteria of essential nutrients, and drastically lowers the pH of the water, creating an intensely acidic medium. This acid environment precipitates a chemical process identical to commercial leather manufacture: human skin and keratinous tissues (such as hair and nails) are tanned into a supple, dark-brown leather. Conversely, the high acidity completely dissolves calcium phosphate, frequently causing the internal skeleton and teeth to disappear entirely.

Paragraph 3. The most celebrated bog body is Tollund Man, unearthed by peat cutters in a Danish bog near Silkeborg in May 1950. Buried over 2,400 years ago during the early Iron Age, the man lay curled on his side in an attitude of tranquil rest, wearing a pointed sheepskin cap fastened with a leather chin-strap. His facial features—including individual whiskers on his chin and wrinkles across his brow—remained so pristine that local police initially treated the discovery as a contemporary murder victim. However, a braided leather noose drawn tightly around his neck confirmed that his death was deliberate and violent.

Paragraph 4. A comprehensive modern forensic autopsy of Tollund Man’s intact gastrointestinal system shed extraordinary light on prehistoric subsistence. Analysis of his stomach and intestinal contents revealed that his final meal consisted entirely of a dense porridge prepared from cultivated grains (mainly barley and linseed) intermixed with the seeds of over forty species of wild weeds, including knotweed and wild pansy. Notably, the meal contained no trace of meat, dairy, or fresh summer fruits, indicating that he perished in late winter or early spring before the agricultural emergence of new crops.

Paragraph 5. The underlying motivation behind these ancient bog depositions remains intensely debated by historians. Early nineteenth-century commentators, influenced by the classical writings of the Roman historian Tacitus, viewed bog individuals as executed criminals, military cowards, or social outcasts cast out into wetlands as legal punishment. However, contemporary osteological and archaeological analysis suggests a far more sacred, ritualistic explanation. Many bog individuals display evidence of the 'triple death'—a ceremonial killing technique combining strangulation, severe bludgeoning, and throat-cutting. Furthermore, the deliberate deposition of valuable bronze weapons, gold ornaments, and imported pottery alongside the bodies strongly points toward ritual human sacrifice, offered by communities to appease fertility goddesses and ensure tribal survival through periods of catastrophic winter famine.

q8.text: Bog bodies retain their soft body tissues better than mummies found in dry deserts.

steps: Đoạn 1: Nêu bog bodies khác với desert mummies vì giữ được mô mềm, nhưng không có câu nào so sánh trực tiếp loại nào giữ tốt hơn (better than).

q9.text: Tollund Man was discovered during an archaeological excavation organised by a local university.

steps: Đoạn 3: Được tìm thấy bởi công nhân cắt than bùn (unearthed by peat cutters), không phải cuộc khai quật của trường đại học.

q10.text: Tollund Man’s stomach contents showed clear evidence of meat consumption shortly before death.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...the meal contained no trace of meat, dairy, or fresh summer fruits..." → Mâu thuẫn trực tiếp với clear evidence of meat consumption.

q11.text: The Roman historian Tacitus wrote about the ritual punishment of criminals in northern Europe.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...influenced by the classical writings of the Roman historian Tacitus, viewed bog individuals as executed criminals, military cowards, or social outcasts cast out into wetlands as legal punishment."

q12.text: Archaeologists have uncovered valuable metal items buried close to some bog bodies.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...the deliberate deposition of valuable bronze weapons, gold ornaments, and imported pottery alongside the bodies..."

q13.text: Most discovered bog bodies have suffered permanent damage due to modern exhibition techniques.

steps: Toàn bài: Bài viết không thảo luận về tác động của kỹ thuật trưng bày bảo tàng hiện đại đối với các xác ướp than bùn.
